root_cause.text: In lib/flex_proportions.c, fprop_new_period() updated the fprop_global seqcount with only preemption disabled instead of IRQs disabled, allowing a hardirq reader to interrupt during write_seqcount_begin()/end() and spin forever on an odd sequence value.
root_cause.evidence: The patch changes fprop_new_period() from preempt_disable_nested()/preempt_enable_nested() to local_irq_save()/local_irq_restore(), and the commit message explicitly describes a hardirq path reaching fprop_fraction_percpu() where read_seqcount_begin(&p->sequence) “sees odd sequence so loops indefinitely,” noting this was introduced by “remove local_irq_ops in fprop_new_period().”

agent_logs.root_cause_candidate: In lib/flex_proportions.c, fprop_new_period() updated the fprop_global seqcount with only preemption disabled instead of IRQs disabled, allowing a hardirq reader to interrupt during write_seqcount_begin()/end() and spin forever on an odd sequence value.
agent_logs.evidence_points: The patch changes fprop_new_period() from preempt_disable_nested()/preempt_enable_nested() to local_irq_save()/local_irq_restore(), and the commit message explicitly describes a hardirq path reaching fprop_fraction_percpu() where read_seqcount_begin(&p->sequence) “sees odd sequence so loops indefinitely,” noting this was introduced by “remove local_irq_ops in fprop_new_period().”

intent_record.intent_summary: Disable local interrupts instead of only preemption before beginning the seqcount write section in fprop_new_period() to correctly protect the update.
intent_record.what: The function fprop_new_period() adds a new local variable `unsigned long flags;` and replaces the call to `preempt_disable_nested()` with `local_irq_save(flags)` before `write_seqcount_begin(&p->sequence)`.
intent_record.how: At runtime, this changes the protection around the seqcount write-side critical section from disabling preemption to disabling local interrupts and saving interrupt state, preventing interrupt-context concurrency while updating the sequence-protected data.

intent_record.intent_summary: Restore local interrupt state instead of only reenabling preemption when finishing fprop_new_period().
intent_record.what: The call to preempt_enable_nested() at the end of fprop_new_period() was replaced with a call to local_irq_restore(flags), using a previously saved interrupt state instead of only reenabling nested preemption.
intent_record.how: At runtime, the function now restores the CPU's local interrupt state on exit from the protected update section rather than merely reenabling preemption, ensuring interrupts are returned to their prior state after the seqcount-protected period/event update and preventing incorrect interrupt state handling.

grouping_result.intent: Restore local interrupt state instead of only reenabling preemption when finishing fprop_new_period().

consistency_review.core_intent: Correct fprop_new_period()'s seqcount update protection by using local interrupt save/restore around the write section instead of only disabling and reenabling preemption.

relevance_review.reason: The changes directly fix the root cause by replacing preemption-only protection with local IRQ save/restore around the seqcount write in fprop_new_period(), preventing hardirq readers from observing an interrupted odd sequence value.

candidates.rationale: This is the core flawed protection: it disables preemption but not local IRQs before entering the seqcount write-side critical section, allowing a hardirq reader to interrupt while the seqcount is odd.
Beginning the seqcount write section without IRQs disabled exposes readers in hardirq context to observing an in-progress odd sequence and potentially spinning forever.
This matching restoration shows the whole critical section relied only on preemption disable/enable rather than IRQ save/restore, confirming the incorrect protection model that caused the race.

vuln_statements.explanation: This statement is the root cause: it disables only preemption before entering the seqcount write-side critical section, leaving hard IRQs enabled. A hardirq reader can interrupt while the seqcount is odd and spin indefinitely.
This begins the seqcount write section under insufficient protection because only preemption, not local IRQs, was disabled. That allows hardirq readers to observe the in-progress odd sequence value.

This matching unlock-side statement confirms the critical section used preemption disable/enable instead of IRQ-safe protection, completing the vulnerable pattern that allowed the seqcount race with hardirq readers.

However, there is no IRQ disabling or lock/irqsave protection in this writer path.
